# Set Plot

> Set Plot is a browser-based planning tool for film and photo shoots: lighting diagrams to scale, storyboards and animatics, shoot notes, and a PDF with the call sheet, shot list and gear list. Made by Malik Motion in Randers, Denmark. Free during the open alpha.

## Product
- [Set Plot](https://plot.malikmotion.com/): lighting diagram maker, storyboard tool and shoot planner for cinematographers, gaffers, photographers, directors and producers
- [What’s new](https://plot.malikmotion.com/changelog.html): product updates

## Set Plot Academy (free filmmaking lessons)
- [Academy overview](https://plot.malikmotion.com/academy/): all lessons, grouped by topic
- [Three-point lighting: key, fill and back light explained](https://plot.malikmotion.com/academy/three-point-lighting/): Three-point lighting uses three lights around a subject: a key light about 45° to one side of the camera, a softer fill light on the other side to control how dark the shadows get, and a back light behind the subject to separate them from the background. It’s the starting point for interviews, portraits and most dialogue scenes.
- [Rembrandt lighting: how to get the triangle of light](https://plot.malikmotion.com/academy/rembrandt-lighting/): Rembrandt lighting puts the key light about 45° to the side and 45° above the subject’s face, so the nose shadow joins the cheek shadow and leaves a small triangle of light under the eye on the shadow side. It needs only one light and gives a moody, painterly portrait.
- [Butterfly lighting (Paramount lighting) for beauty and portraits](https://plot.malikmotion.com/academy/butterfly-lighting/): Butterfly lighting places the key light directly in front of the face and above the camera, pointing down, so a small butterfly-shaped shadow falls under the nose. A white bounce below the chin fills the shadows under the eyes and jaw. It flatters cheekbones and is the classic beauty and glamour look.
- [Split lighting: half the face in light, half in shadow](https://plot.malikmotion.com/academy/split-lighting/): Split lighting places the key light 90° to the side of the subject at face height, so exactly half the face is lit and the other half falls into shadow. It’s the most dramatic of the portrait patterns and is used for villains, inner conflict and moody music videos.
- [High-key vs low-key lighting: what’s the difference?](https://plot.malikmotion.com/academy/high-key-and-low-key-lighting/): High-key lighting is bright, even and low in contrast, with a light background and soft shadows: think commercials and sitcoms. Low-key lighting is dark and high in contrast, with deep shadows and little fill: think noir and thrillers. The difference comes down to the key-to-fill ratio and how bright the background is.
- [How to light with a window: natural light for film and photo](https://plot.malikmotion.com/academy/window-light/): To light with a window, place the subject side-on or at 45° to the window so it acts as a soft key light, shoot from the room side so the light wraps toward the camera, and add a white bounce on the opposite side for fill. If the sun hits the window directly, diffuse it with a frame or a sheer curtain.
- [Interview lighting setup: a two-camera interview, step by step](https://plot.malikmotion.com/academy/interview-lighting/): A good interview setup uses a large soft key on the side the subject looks toward, negative fill on the camera side to keep shape, a back light for separation, and practicals in the background for depth. Run an A camera on a medium shot and a B camera on a tighter angle so you can cut between them.
- [Product lighting: a tabletop setup for packshots](https://plot.malikmotion.com/academy/product-lighting/): A clean product setup uses a white sweep behind the product, a strip softbox as the key to draw a long highlight down one side, a bounce on the other side for fill and a gridded rim light from behind to outline the edges. Use a longer lens and a smaller aperture so the whole product stays sharp.
- [Color temperature on set: mixing daylight, tungsten and practicals](https://plot.malikmotion.com/academy/color-temperature/): Color temperature describes how warm or cool light is, measured in Kelvin (K). Tungsten and household lamps are warm (2700–3200K), daylight is cool (5600K and up). Set the camera’s white balance to the source you want to look neutral, and use CTO gels to warm a light or CTB gels to cool it so mixed sources look intentional.
- [The 180-degree rule: keeping screen direction consistent](https://plot.malikmotion.com/academy/180-degree-rule/): The 180-degree rule says that in a scene between two people, the camera should stay on one side of an imaginary line drawn between them (the axis of action). Keep every camera on that side and each person stays on the same side of the frame from shot to shot. Cross the line and they appear to swap places, which confuses viewers.
- [How to make a lighting diagram (and why every shoot needs one)](https://plot.malikmotion.com/academy/lighting-diagram/): A lighting diagram is a top-down plan of a setup showing the room, the talent and their marks, the camera and lens, every light with its fixture, modifier, power and colour temperature, the grip (flags, frames, bounces) and any notes. A good diagram lets a gaffer build the setup without asking you a single question.
- [How to make a shot list and storyboard for a shoot](https://plot.malikmotion.com/academy/shot-list-and-storyboard/): A shot list is a numbered list of every shot you plan to film, with shot size, angle, lens, movement and a short description. A storyboard draws those shots as frames so everyone can see the sequence. Make the shot list first from the script, sketch the frames, then plan the camera positions on a top-down diagram so you can shoot in the most efficient order.
- [Getting started with Set Plot: your first lighting plan in 5 minutes](https://plot.malikmotion.com/academy/set-plot-getting-started/): In Set Plot every job is a shoot, and every lighting setup in it is a setup with its own plan. Start from a template or a blank sheet, add lights, grip, camera and talent from the left toolbar, select anything to edit it in the inspector, press Z to fit everything in view, and export a plot sheet from Export.
- [Placing lights, grip and beams in Set Plot](https://plot.malikmotion.com/academy/set-plot-lights-and-grip/): Add a light from Lights (1), drag it into place and drag its handle to aim it. Select it to set the fixture, modifier (M), power and Kelvin, and use the slider above the light for quick power changes. Press B to show or hide beams, I for fixture specs, and [ / ] to turn in 15° steps.
- [Drawing rooms, windows and locations in Set Plot](https://plot.malikmotion.com/academy/set-plot-rooms-and-locations/): Open Set (5) to draw the space: walls, windows, doors, curtains, sheers, furniture and backdrops. Drag a wall’s corners to resize it, slide curtains along a window, and add the sun and a sun path to see where daylight comes from. For exteriors, drop in a satellite map and plan on top of it.
- [Notes, to-dos, cards and mind maps in Set Plot](https://plot.malikmotion.com/academy/set-plot-notes-and-mind-maps/): The right toolbar adds cards next to the plan: notes (Shift + 1), to-dos (Shift + 2), comments (Shift + 3), tables, colours, columns, images and Google Docs. Any note becomes a mind map: press Tab to add a connected idea, ⌘/Ctrl + Enter for one at the same level, and F to fold a branch.
- [Storyboards and animatics in Set Plot](https://plot.malikmotion.com/academy/set-plot-storyboards/): Open a storyboard frame to draw with Photoshop-style tools (V move, B brush, E eraser, U shapes, T type). Once you have two or more frames, press Make animatic to open a Resolve-style timeline: play with Space or J K L, cut with ⌘/Ctrl + B, set in and out with I and O, and add voice-over and music from the media pool. Everything saves automatically.
- [Animating storyboard layers with keyframes in Set Plot](https://plot.malikmotion.com/academy/set-plot-keyframe-animation/): In the storyboard editor, click Animate on a layer to put it on the timeline. Add keyframes for position, scale, rotation and opacity with ⌥/Alt + Shift + P, S, R or T, press U to reveal the keyframed properties, drag keyframes to change timing, and ease them with F9. Shift + F3 opens the speed graph.
- [Working with your crew in Set Plot: sharing, chat and comments](https://plot.malikmotion.com/academy/set-plot-collaboration/): Click Share to add people to a shoot by email with view, edit or admin rights; they get an email invite, even if they don’t have an account yet. Plan together live with cursors and follow mode, talk in the chat with @mentions and #tags for objects, leave comment threads, save named versions, and send clients a view-only link.
- [Exporting from Set Plot: plot sheets, call sheets and gear lists](https://plot.malikmotion.com/academy/set-plot-exporting/): Open Export for a PNG or SVG plot sheet with legend and scale, a power budget sheet for the gaffer, a copied gear list, or one PDF with the call sheet, shot list, gear list and lighting plots for the whole shoot. On the day, Shift + F hides the toolbars for a clean view on a tablet.
- [Set Plot keyboard shortcuts: the complete cheat sheet](https://plot.malikmotion.com/academy/set-plot-keyboard-shortcuts/): Press ? in Set Plot to see every shortcut. The essentials: Z fit, Shift + A search and add, 1–6 left toolbar, Shift + 1–9 right toolbar, B beams, S snap, M modifier, [ ] rotate, ⌘/Ctrl + D duplicate, X delete. Click Customize in the shortcuts window to change any of them.
